title: Overtime tiers inside a crew's labor budget

blocks.text: A water utility plans next month's work for its contracted main-repair crew. Each job in `jobs` needs a known number of crew hours. The contract prices the crew's hours in tiers, given in `tiers` as `(hours up to, $ per hour)`, in order:
So a month of 170 hours costs 160 × 60 + 10 × 90. The contract allows no more hours than the last tier's limit. The month's labor cost must not exceed `budget` dollars.

The model in `crew_month.py` has a binary `x[jid]` per job (1 if the job is done this month). Write `add_labor_rules(model, x, jobs, tiers, budget)` so that the model allows exactly the months (which jobs) whose real labor cost fits the budget and whose hours stay within the contract. Add whatever variables you need. Work from `tiers`, not from the numbers in the table: the tests use other tiers too.
With $`J`$ the jobs and $`h_j`$ the hours of job $`j`$, the model so far is

Write the month's hours as an expression first. Then write its labor cost as a function of the hours: what shape is it, and does the budget row press that cost up or down? That decides whether you need anything more than continuous variables.
The tests fix which jobs are done and ask the solver whether the model accepts the month, so any correct formulation passes. About eight lines.

from __future__ import annotations

from dataclasses import dataclass

from ortools.math_opt.python import mathopt


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Job:
    jid: str
    hours: float


def add_labor_rules(model: mathopt.Model, x: dict, jobs: list[Job], tiers: list[tuple[float, float]],
                    budget: float) -> None:
    """The month's tiered labor cost within the budget, and no more hours than the last tier allows."""
    hours = sum(j.hours * x[j.jid] for j in jobs)
    used, cost, start = [], 0, 0.0
    for k, (upper, rate) in enumerate(tiers):
        part = model.add_variable(lb=0, ub=upper - start, name=f"tier{k}")   # hours paid at this rate
        used.append(part)
        cost = cost + rate * part
        start = upper
    model.add_linear_constraint(hours == sum(used), name="hours")
    model.add_linear_constraint(cost <= budget, name="labor_budget")


def build(jobs: list[Job], tiers: list[tuple[float, float]], budget: float) -> tuple[mathopt.Model, dict]:
    model = mathopt.Model(name="crew month")
    x = {j.jid: model.add_binary_variable(name=f"x_{j.jid}") for j in jobs}
    add_labor_rules(model, x, jobs, tiers, budget)
    model.maximize(sum(j.hours * x[j.jid] for j in jobs))
    return model, x


if __name__ == "__main__":
    jobs = [Job("Elm St", 100), Job("Oak Ave", 80), Job("Pine Rd", 40)]
    model, x = build(jobs, [(160, 60.0), (200, 90.0), (240, 120.0)], 12_000)
    print(model.get_num_linear_constraints(), "rows")

cases.says: a month of regular hours within the budget is allowed, and a month whose tiered labor cost exceeds it is refused
a month inside the last tier is allowed with a large budget, and one past it is refused
a month that would fit if every hour were paid the regular rate, but not at the overtime rate, is refused
a month reaching 30 hours into the top tier is refused when the budget only covers 20 of them

origin.section: The Same Cost Is the Largest of Its Lines

concepts: a piecewise-linear function is fixed by its breakpoints, and its slopes tell convex from concave
a convex cost written as one row per segment's line, inside a budget row
a convex cost written as one bounded variable per segment, with no binaries
